title: Checking for Alerts
unit: CS-ICT251101 Monitor and Report Cyber Threats

parts.html:
At the end of this session, you should be able to:

  1. Explain what a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) is and why alert intake follows one.
  2. Receive and record detection alerts from SIEM, AV, firewall, WAF, DLP, EDR and NDR as per SOP (PC 1.1).
  3. Receive and record incident reports made by phone, walk-in, email, SMS, chat and video conference (PC 1.2).
  4. Check detections for ransomware and PE infection (virus) red flags as per SOP (PC 1.3).
  5. Recognize social engineering attempts during intake and respond as per SOP.

Checking for alerts is the first element of monitoring and reporting cyber threats. A monitoring analyst receives every alert and every report, records it completely, and checks it at once for red flags. Each organization writes these steps in a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), so that every analyst on every shift does the same thing, in the same order, within the same time limits. In the lab you follow SOC-SOP-01 Alert and Report Intake (~/day5/soc_alert_sop.txt).

  1. Receive — take the detection alert from the queue, or the report from a person (PC 1.1, 1.2).
  2. Record — write down the facts the SOP asks for, without judging yet.
  3. Check red flags — compare what you see with the SOP red flag list (PC 1.3). Red flags are escalated immediately.
  4. Hand over — assessment against pre-identified criteria and ticketing follow on Day 6 (PC 1.4, 1.5).

A detection alert is a message from a security solution saying it saw something suspicious. The Competency Standards list seven sources. They all arrive in the SOC alert queue, usually through the SIEM.

Detection Alert (CS)What It ReportsExample from the Day 5 Queue
SIEM alertCorrelated events from many logs"18 logon failures then success on DC-01"
AV alertMalware found on an endpoint"Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml quarantined"
Firewall alertTraffic allowed or denied by rules"Inbound RDP denied (64 attempts in 5 min)"
Web application firewall (WAF) alertAttacks against websites"SQL injection blocked on /loan/apply.php"
DLP alertSensitive data leaving the organization"Payroll file uploaded to personal cloud storage"
EDR alertSuspicious behavior on an endpoint"Mass file rename by unsigned process"
NDR alertSuspicious network behavior"Unusual SMB writes to \\FS-01\Installers"

Acknowledge on Time

To acknowledge an alert means to take ownership of it: you change its status from New to Acknowledged so that everyone knows someone is working on it. The SOP sets a time limit for each severity. Missing it is an SLA breach (SLA = service level agreement).

SeverityAcknowledge Within (SOC-SOP-01 rule A2)
Critical15 minutes
High30 minutes
Medium120 minutes
Low480 minutes (8 hours)
InformationalNo acknowledgment needed (auto-closed)
TIP
Waiting time = now − received time. Alert Q-5006 (High) was received at 08:33:40. At 09:30 it has waited 56 minutes, which is more than 30, so it is an SLA breach: acknowledge it at once and tell the Shift Lead. Always use the same time zone (Philippine Standard Time, UTC+8).

What to Record for Every Alert

  • Alert ID, time received, and time acknowledged
  • Source (SIEM, AV, firewall, WAF, DLP, EDR, NDR) and product
  • Host (affected computer) and rule or detection name
  • Severity and status
  • Whether it matches a red flag

Not every threat is found by a tool. Employees, customers and partners also report what they see. The Competency Standards list six channels for a detection report:

Channel (CS)ExampleIntake Tip
Phone callAn accountant calls: "my files end in .lockd"Write their exact words; confirm the callback number
Walk-inAn engineer comes to the SOC deskAsk what they did and when; note the PC name
EmailA branch forwards a suspicious emailAsk them to forward it as an attachment; do not click links
SMS"IT" asks the SOC to text an OTPTreat requests for passwords or OTPs as social engineering
ChatA user reports a printer jamNot a security matter: redirect to the IT Helpdesk
Video conferenceA fake "virus warning" pop-up is shared on screenRecord what you saw; tell them not to call the number

The Intake Record

  • Report ID, channel, date and time received
  • Reporter name, department and callback number from the company directory
  • What they saw, in their own words
  • Affected computer, account or device
  • What they already did (clicked, opened, restarted)
NOTE — Social engineering during intake
Attackers also contact the SOC. Never ask for, or give, a password or one-time PIN (OTP). Verify phone, SMS and chat reporters by calling back the number in the company directory, not the number that contacted you. Record only the personal data the SOP needs (Data Privacy Act, RA 10173).

The Competency Standards name two red flag detections that must be checked at once: ransomware and PE infection (virus). Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment; it can stop a bank branch, school or hospital within minutes. A PE infection is a file-infector virus: it inserts its code into Portable Executable files (.exe, .dll), so every copy of an infected installer spreads it further.

CodeRed FlagWhat You SeeWhere
R1RansomwareMany files renamed with the same new extension in a short timeEDR file events, file shares
R2RansomwareA ransom note file appears (README_RESTORE_FILES.txt, HOW_TO_DECRYPT.txt)Desktop, Documents, shares
R3RansomwareShadow copy or backup deletion attempt (vssadmin delete shadows, wbadmin delete catalog)EDR process events
R4RansomwareA detection name that contains "Ransom"AV / EDR alerts
V1PE infectionMany .exe or .dll files modified that should not change, by a non-updater processEDR file events
V2PE infectionA detection name that starts with "Virus:" (file infector)AV alerts
V3PE infectionThe same detection on several hosts that used the same shared folderAV alerts, SIEM

Look-alikes That Are NOT Red Flags

Some approved software does similar things: a backup agent creates thousands of archive files, and Windows Update replaces DLLs in System32. Check the process name and its signer (the company that digitally signed the program) against the SOP approved list. In the lab: scbackup.exe signed by SafeCopy Software Inc., and TiWorker.exe signed by Microsoft Windows. An unsigned program in a Temp or Downloads folder doing the same thing is a red flag.

TIP — First response to suspected ransomware (Level I)
Ask the user to unplug the network cable or turn off Wi-Fi. Do NOT shut the PC down: evidence in memory is lost. Never pay or contact the attacker. Escalate immediately to the Shift Lead by phone, then record it. The Shift Lead decides on isolation.

Antivirus and EDR tools scan in different ways and take different actions. Knowing them helps you read an alert correctly.

Scan or ActionMeaning
Real-time (on-access) protectionChecks each file when it is opened, downloaded or run
Quick scanChecks the places malware usually hides (memory, startup, system folders)
Full scanChecks every file on every drive; slow, used after an infection
Actions (CS Range of Variables)Failed, Clean, Delete, Quarantine, Blocked, Re-image

TermMeaning
SOPStandard Operating Procedure: the written, approved steps every analyst follows
AcknowledgeTake ownership of an alert so everyone knows it is being handled
SLA breachMissing the time limit the SOP sets for a severity
Detection reportA report of a possible incident from a person (phone, walk-in, email, SMS, chat, video conference)
Red flag detectionA detection the SOP says must be escalated at once (ransomware, PE infection)
PE filePortable Executable: a Windows program or library (.exe, .dll)
SignerThe company that digitally signed a program; unsigned programs deserve a closer look
Social engineeringTricking people, including SOC staff, into giving access or information
